sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Annwn, also called Annwyn and Annwfn, is a Welsh mythological site. The Welsh, like the Irish, offered several places for the Otherworld. Annwn means abyss. The Welsh saw it as a castle by the sea, called Caer Siddi. They also saw it as a court of intoxication, called Caer Feddwid, and as a palace of glass, called Caer Wydyr. Like Tir na nOg, the Irish island of the blessed, Annwn was a place of sweetness and charm. Its people did not age and did not suffer. They ate their fill from a magic cauldron. They quenched their thirst at an ever-flowing well. Two kings ruled Annwn. They were Arawn and Hafgan, and they were perpetually at war. Arawn figures more prominently in legend.
